newsitem.title: USA: Specialists, high technology cut death rate - study.
newsitem.headline: Specialists, high technology cut death rate - study.

text.p: Insurance companies may save money by encouraging primary care physicians to care for people with heart problems but the policy may cost lives, according to two studies to be published Thursday.
About 1.5 million Americans a year suffer heart attacks. About 750,000 are taken to hospitals and about one-third of those die, the American Heart Association says.

In the first study, Dr. James Jollis and colleagues at Duke University Medical Center in North Carolina found that heart disease patients treated by a cardiologist were 12 percent less likely to die within a year than those treated by a general practitioner.

In the second, a team led by Dr. Joe Selby of the Kaiser Permanente Medical Care Program in Oakland, California, found that the death rate was one-third lower among patients treated in hospitals that tended to use a high-tech -- albeit expensive -- procedure known as angiography to test the heart.
Both were in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.

"The data from both these reports suggest that cardiac specialists and the procedures they perform are beneficial to patients," said Dr. Lee Goldman of the University of California at San Francisco in an editorial in the Journal.

"The study validates the saying that practice makes perfect, said Daniel Mark, a member of the Duke team. "It stands to reason that a doctor who focuses on hearts would likely provide a different level of care than those who treat a wide variety of diseases."

But in recent years some insurance companies have been limiting access to specialists, including heart specialists known as cardiologists, in an effort to save money and discourage the use of costly procedures such as angiography.

The Duke study confirmed that care from a cardiologist tends to cost more but it it also saves more lives, Jollis said, perhaps because "patients treated by cardiologists are more likely to receive survival-prolonging medications, including thrombolytic therapy, beta blockers and aspirin."
The results from the Jollis team were developed from the case files of 8,241 patients in hospitals for a heart attack in four states -- Alabama, Connecticut, Iowa and Wisconsin.

The findings of the Selby study were based on followups of 6,851 heart attack patients in 16 Kaiser Permanente hospitals between 1990 and 1992. It found the patient had a better chance of survival when a hospital did angiography frequently.
In addition, when the hospital closely adhered to national guidelines that recommend when angiography should be done, the reduction in the death rate was the most pronounced.
